Subject: Dental Materials
Question: False about polymer crosslinking?
Option A: Crosslinking of low molecular weight polymer increase softening temperature
Option B: Crosslinking of high molecular weight polymer has modest increase in softening temperature
Explanation:
'D' [Phillips' 12th ed 96]

Crosslinking forms bridges between chains and dramatically increases molecular weight. Consequently, physical and mechanical properties vary with the composition and extent of crosslinking for a given polymer system.

• The three-dimensional network of crosslinked polymers increases rigidity and resistance to solvents.
• Crosslinking of a low-molecular-weight polymer increases the softening temperature, known as the glass-transition temperature, compared with that of a high-molecular-weight polymer.
• On the other hand, crosslinking has only a modest influence on strength.

Question: When palladium added to gold alloy, all of the following happens except:
Explanation:
'C' [Phillips' 12th ed 373]

Palladium is a noble metal of the platinum group in the periodic table of elements. Effects of adding palladium to gold:

• Palladium increases the strength, hardness, resistance to corrosion and tarnishing.
• In addition, it increases elastic modulus, strength and hardness of gold alloys and reduces their density.
• Palladium increases melting range and improves its resistance to sag.
• It has a great ability of bleaching (whitening), so that the alloy with 90% gold and 10% of palladium has platinum color.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: In stress-strain curve, 1,2,3,4 represent
Explanation:
'A' [Phillips' 12th ed 32]

Curves depicting shear stress versus shear strain rate are used to characterize the viscous behaviour of fluids. The rheologic behaviours of four types of fluids are shown in the above figure.

Curve 1: Some classes of materials behave like a rigid body until some minimum value of shear stress is reached. This is represented by the offset along the shear-stress axis. These fluids, which exhibit rigid behavior initially and then attain constant viscosity, are referred to as plastic. Ketchup is a familiar example - a sharp blow to the bottle is usually required to produce an initial flow.

Curve 2: Liquids that show the opposite behavior are dilatant and become more rigid as the rate of deformation (shear strain rate) increases. That is, the faster they are stirred, the more viscous and resistant to flow they become.

Curve 3: An "ideal" fluid produces a shear stress proportional to the strain rate. That is, the greater the force applied, the faster the fluid flows and the plot is a straight line. This is known as Newtonian viscosity. Newtonian fluid has a constant viscosity and exhibits a constant slope of shear stress plotted against strain rate, as seen in figure. The plot is a straight line and resembles the elastic portion of a stress-strain curve.

Curve 4: The viscosity of many dental materials decreases with increasing strain rate until it reaches a nearly constant value. That is, the faster they are stirred, forced through a syringe, or squeezed, the less viscous and more fluid they become. This is pseudoplastic viscosity.
Image Reference: Stress-strain curve graph (Shear suess, τ vs Strain rate, ε) with 4 curves labelled 1–4 – Page 81

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: True about hydroquinone
Explanation:
'B' [Phillips' 12th ed 105]

• The addition of a small amount of a common inhibitor, such as hydroquinone, to the monomer inhibits spontaneous polymerization if no initiator is present and retards the polymerization in the presence of an initiator.
• Thus, inhibitors affect both the storage stability and the working time of a dental resin.
• For this reason, commercial dental resins commonly contain a small amount (approximately 0.006% or less) of an inhibitor such as the methyl ether of hydroquinone to aid in the prevention of polymerization during storage and, in the case of two-part (self-cure) systems, to provide adequate time for mixing and placement.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: The difference between the energy required to activate the wire by deflection and that released by it during deactivation is?
Explanation:
'B' [Craig 14th ed 37]

Properties of nickel titanium alloys are Hysteresis, Shape memory, and Super elasticity.

Hysteresis: When the wire is activated and the amount of force increases, the alloy transforms from the austenitic to the martensitic phase. When the force is removed, the wire follows a different path below that of activation and returns to the austenitic structure. The difference between these curves is called hysteresis. This defines the difference between the force given for activation and the force applied by the wire during deactivation. This also shows the level of force a wire delivers to the tooth. Clinically, low hysteresis is desired.

• Shape memory- refers to the ability of the material to "remember" its original shape after being plastically deformed while in the martensitic form. This property is also called Thermoelasticity.

• Super elasticity- Ability of a wire to deliver a near constant force over a wide range of activation. If stress is induced in the nickel-titanium alloy, the austenitic form changed to a martensitic form.

Note: Bauschinger effect is seen in stainless steel wires. It describes the reduction in yield stress of a metal when the direction of deformation is reversed.
Image Reference: Hysteresis graph (Stress vs Strain with Loading and Unloading curves) – Page 84

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: A patient wearing heat cure acrylic denture base, complains of burning sensation after 6 months of denture delivery. The most probable cause of his discomfort is?
Explanation:
'B' [Identification of complete denture problems: a summary. British Dental Journal 2000; 189: 128–134]

The most common and frequently reported a problem with the patients having allergic reactions to denture base acrylic resin is mouth soreness and burning sensation. Areas presenting with burning sensation include the palate, tongue, oral mucosa, and the oropharynx.

The symptoms may be related to higher residual monomer content of acrylic. If excess residual monomer detected, it is advised to rebase the denture using controlled heat cure cycle. Also the dentist may need to consider remaking denture using polycarbonate resin.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Which of the following statement regarding fineness of gold is not correct?
Option A: Fineness means gold content in noble metal alloys by the number of parts of gold per 1000 parts of alloy
Option B: Term carat and fineness are currently used to describe the gold content of current dental alloys
Option C: Carat specifies gold content of an alloys based on parts of gold per 24 part of alloy
Explanation:
'B' [Phillips' 12th ed 368]

Fineness is more practical than karat. Karat is parts of pure gold in 24 parts of alloy. Fineness means gold content in noble metal alloys by the number of parts of gold per 1000 parts of alloy. For example, pure gold has a fineness of 1000, and a 750 fine alloy has a gold content of 75%.

Explanation:

Boric oxide (B₂O₃) can behave as a glass modifier in ceramics to:

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Not true regarding divestment
Option C: Colloidal silica is added to it
Explanation:
'A' [Phillips' 12th ed 212]

Divestment:
• Divestment is a combination of die material and commercially available gypsum-bonded investing medium.
• Divestment is mixed with colloidal silica and die is made from this mix & and a wax pattern is constructed on it. After this, the wax pattern with die is invested in divestment.
• As the entire assembly (die and pattern) is invested in the divestment (normally the wax pattern is removed from the die and invested separately), it eliminates possibility of distortion of wax pattern while removing it from die.
• Because this type of investment is a gypsum-bonded material, it is not recommended for high-fusing alloys used for metal-ceramic restorations. However, it is a highly accurate technique for use with conventional gold alloys, especially those selected for extracoronal preparations.

Question: To reduce the diameter of gypsum die, what would you do

Additional accelerator (potassium sulfate) and retarder (borax) can be added to the gauging water to reduce the setting expansion of the type IV die stone to less than 0.1%, which reduces the diameter of the die.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: In glass transition temperature of wax, what is false-
Option A: There is sudden expansion after it
Option B: Wax is more elastic after it
Option C: It is due to the rearrangement in crystalline structure of wax
Explanation:
'B' [Phillips' 12th ed 198]

Glass transition temperature:
• It is the temperature above which a sharp increase in the thermal expansion coefficient occurs, indicating increased molecular mobility. For inlay wax it is approximately 35 °C
• Some constituents of the wax probably change in their crystalline form at this temperature, and the wax is more plastic at higher temperatures.
• Not all waxes exhibit transition temperatures.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Not true about flux
Option C: Reduce any oxide present, expose clean metal
Explanation:
'D' [Phillips' 12th ed 389]

Flux is a compound applied to metal surfaces that dissolves or prevents the formation of oxides during the melting of an alloy, therefore assisting in the flow of the alloy. Flux doesn't form oxide film.

Purpose of flux:
• Surface Protection: Covers the metal surface and prevents access to oxygen so no oxides can form.
• Reducing Agent: Reduces any oxides present and exposes clean metal Solvent.
• Dissolves any oxides present and carries them away.

Fluxes for use with noble metal alloys are generally based on boric acid, boric anhydride, and borax. Chromium oxides that form on base metal alloys are more stable and fluoride containing fluxes are used as solvents to dissolve chromium, nickel, and cobalt oxides.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Not true about use of excessive flux
Option C: Removed excess by boiling in HCL for 5 minutes
Explanation:
'C' [Phillips' 12th ed 389]

• It is of primary importance to minimize the amount of flux used. Entrapment of flux within the filler metal can cause a weakened joint (Option D).
• Residual flux that is covered with porcelain can cause discoloration and bubbling of the porcelain (Options A & B).
• Flux combines with metal oxides and forms a glass during the soldering process, and the residue should be removed. Sandblasting the joint immediately after removal from the soldering investment with alumina abrasive particles and boiling in water for about 5 minutes are recommended. So, Option C is wrong.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Pick the wrong statement in relation to dispersion strengthening
Option D: Variety of dispersed crystalline phases are used to strengthen the ceramics
Explanation:
'B' [Phillips' 12th ed 454]

The major drawbacks of ceramics are brittleness, low fracture toughness and low tensile strength. Dispersion strengthening is one of the approaches to increase the strength of ceramics.

Dispersion strengthening of glasses:
• Dental ceramics that contains glass phase (option A) can be strengthened by dispersion strengthening i.e. dispersing ceramic crystals of high strength and elasticity such as leucite, lithium disilicate, alumina, magnesia-alumina, spinel, zirconia in the glass matrix (option D).
• When crystal materials are added in the glassy phase, a strong glass-crystal composition is obtained, thus durability and fracture resistance increases. So it prevents or inhibit propagation of cracks (option C).
• Toughening depends on the crystal type, its size, its volume fraction, the interparticle spacing, and its relative coefficient of thermal expansion relative to the glass matrix.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: What occurs if Gypsum is heated above 700 degree C
Option B: Breakdown of CaSO4 which affect gold alloy
Option C: Breakdown of Na2So4 which affect gold alloy
Explanation:
'B' [Phillips' 10th ed 472]

Gypsum-bonded investments are used for casting gold alloys. These can withstand a temperature of 700°C. If gypsum investment is heated about 700°C, decomposition of CaSO₄ occurs with emission of SO₂ gas. This not only causes shrinkage of the investment but also contaminates the gold castings with the sulphides of the non-noble elements such as silver and copper. So gypsum investments should not be heated above 700°C.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Strength of set gypsum is expressed as
Explanation:
'D' [Phillips' 12th ed 188]

The strength of set gypsum products is generally expressed in terms of compressive strength, although diametral tensile strength should also be considered to determine the overall strength characteristics.

Effect of water content on strength:
• Two strength properties of gypsum are reported: the wet strength (also known as green strength), and the dry strength.
• The wet strength is the strength that is determined when water in excess of that required for hydration of the hemihydrate remains in the test specimen.
• When such excess water is removed by drying, the strength obtained is the dry strength. The dry strength may be two or more times as high as the wet strength.

Effect of W/P ratio on strength:
• Material that is mixed at a high W/P ratio has a diametral tensile strength as high as 25% of the corresponding compressive strength.
• When materials are mixed at low W/P ratios, the diametral tensile strength is less than 10% of the corresponding compressive strength.

Effect of manipulation and additives on strength:
The addition of an accelerator or retarder lowers both the wet strength and the dry strength of the gypsum product.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Test for measuring the tensile strength of brittle material
Explanation:
'B' [Phillips' 12th ed 58]

• Tensile strength can generally be determined by subjecting a rod, wire, or dumbbell-shaped specimen to tensile loading (a uniaxial tension test). Since this test is quite difficult to perform for brittle materials because of alignment and gripping problems, another test can be used to determine this property for brittle dental materials. It is referred to as the diametral compression test.
• Brazilian cylinder splitting test is type of diametral compression test and is the widely used test to determine the ultimate tensile strength of brittle materials. This test should be used only for materials that exhibit elastic deformation primarily and little or no plastic deformation.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: GIC colour and clinical appearance is determined by
Explanation:
'B' [Phillips' 12th ed 320-21]

Effect of Glass composition on colour and visual appearance:
• The glass composition in GIC contains silica, calcium, alumina, and fluoride.
• The ratio of alumina to silica is the key to their reactivity with polyacrylic acid. Visual appearance is dependent upon the ratio of silica to alumina. Glasses high in silica are transparent while those high in alumina are opaque.
• Barium, strontium, or other higher atomic number metal oxides are added to the glass to increase the radiopacity.

Effect of viscosity of liquid: Controls working and setting time of the cement.

Effect of tartaric acid:
• Tartaric acid is a rate-controlling additive in the GIC liquid that allows a wider range of glasses to be used
• It improves the handling properties and decreases viscosity
• It lengthens shelf life before gelling of the liquid occurs
• It increases working time, and shortens the setting time

Effect of Powder particles size: controls the film thickness of the cement. The bigger the particle size, the thicker will be the film of the cement.

Explanation:

The chief disadvantage of the type IV gypsum die is its susceptibility to abrasion during carving of the wax pattern. Several means are used to increase the abrasion resistance include:

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: In porcelain, metal oxide helps in
Explanation:
'A' [Phillips' 12th ed 382]

Function of metal oxide in ceramics:
• Metal oxides such as Al₂O₃, BaO, CaO, K₂O, Li₂O, Na₂O, ZnO, and ZrO₂ are components of either dental core ceramics or dental veneering (layering) ceramics. These oxides contributes to opacification and color to ceramic.
• Metal oxides like alumina increases the fracture toughness by disrupting the propagation of the crack.
• Tin, and indium oxide added to high noble (HN) and noble (N) alloys which are used for metal-ceramic prostheses, helps in promoting bonding between the ceramic veneer and the metal oxide on the metal surface. These metal oxides increase the bond strength between metal and ceramic. They also harden Ag-Pd alloys.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Multiple nodules in the inner surface of casting can be avoided by
Option B: By using surfactant over wax pattern before investing
Explanation:
'C' [Phillips' 12th ed 224]

Surface irregularities are isolated imperfections, such as nodules, that are not characteristic of the entire surface area. Castings with phosphate bonded investments are more prone to such imperfections.

Types of surface irregularities:
• Nodules
• Water films
• fins

Causes of nodules:
• Small nodule - Bubbles of gases (air) trapped between the wax pattern and the investment produce nodules on the casting surface
• Large nodule- Air trapped during investing
• Nodules on occlusal surface – Prolonged vibration after pouring
• Multiple nodules
  - Inadequate vacuum during mixing
  - Improper brush technique
  - Lack of surfactant (wetting agent)

Prevention of nodules:
• By mixing under vacuum (best method). If a manual method is used a mechanical mixer with vibration both before and after mixing should be used.
• By using surfactant over wax pattern before investing. But it is by no means a certain remedy. Precautions while applying wetting agents are:
  - Should be applied in thin layer
  - Air drying the wetting agent, since any excess liquid dilutes the investment, possibly producing surface irregularities on the casting.
• Careful coating of the wax pattern with investment

Explanation:

The ability of a substance or object to spring back into shape when stressed upto proportional limit is called resilience. Popularly, the term resilience is associated with springiness, which means precisely the amount of energy absorbed within a unit volume of a structure when it is stressed to its proportional limit.

The area bounded by the elastic region is a measure of resilience and the total area under the stress-strain curve is a measure of toughness (total elastic+ plastic region).

In the question it is mentioned as below its modulus of elasticity. Elastic modulus is the stress /strain below the proportional limit. So it is the elastic region of the graph (option A, B, D are wrong).

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Sol to gel and gel to conversion is property based on
Explanation:
'B' [Phillips' 12th ed 170]

• The physical change of agar from sol to gel and gel to sol is a function of temperature. The gel liquefies to a sol when it is heated to a temperature known as the liquefaction temperature (70°C to 100°C).
• When the sol is cooled, it becomes a gel at a point known as the gelation temperature (between 37°C and 50°C). Thus, it is called a reversible hydrocolloid.
• The gelation temperature is critical for impression making. If it is too high, the heat from the sol may injure the oral tissues. Conversely, if the gelation temperature is too far below oral temperature, it will be impossible to make the impression because the sol will not covert to a gel.

Question: Transverse contraction strain and longitudinal elongation strain is related by
Explanation:
'B' [Phillips' 12th ed 56]

• Because of the conservation of mass, an object, such as a cylinder, becomes longer and thinner when a tensile force is applied to it. Conversely, a compressive force acts to make such an object shorter and thicker.
• Poisson's ratio is defined as the ratio of the change in the width per unit width of a material, to the change in its length per unit length, as a result of strain.
• Poisson's ratio is the ratio of transverse contraction strain to longitudinal extension strain in the direction of stretching force. Tensile deformation is considered positive and compressive deformation is considered negative.

Poisson's ratio, v = Transverse strain / Longitudinal strain
Poisons ratio = 0.38 x Youngs modulus

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Most accepted theory of setting reaction of gypsum
Explanation:
'A' [Philips' 12th ed 183]

There are three theories of gypsum setting. The colloidal Theory, the hydration theory, and the dissolution-precipitation theory.

The most widely accepted mechanism is the dissolution-precipitation theory, which is based on dissolution of the hemihydrate particles in water followed by instant recrystallization to the dihydrate.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: During electroplating, silver is deposited at
Option D: silver will remain suspended in electrolyte bath
Explanation:
'A' [Craig 13th ed 376]

• The impression is made conductive when the surface is brushed with powdered silver, which adheres well to rubber impressions and it acts as a cathode.
• A pure silver anode is required, with a silver-cyanide plating solution. Care must be taken to avoid the addition of acids to the cyanide solutions, which can cause the release of cyanide vapor, a "death chamber" gas.
• Chemical deposition of silver from a silver nitrate solution can be used if greater surface detail reproduction is desired.
• A current setting of approximately 5 mA is suitable to start the plating of a single-tooth impression (cathode).

Question: Most commonly used monomer in adhesives is?
Explanation:
'A' [Phillips 11th ed 265]

Generally, adhesive resins are composed mainly of hydrophobic dimethacrylates such as Bis-GMA (60-70 wt%), TEGDMA, and UDMA, and a small amount of a hydrophilic monomer such as HEMA (30-40 wt%)

• BisGMA remains the most common monomer used in dental composites and adhesives.
• TEGDMA is the most common diluent monomer used in dental composites and adhesives.

Question: The best pickling solution for gypsum bonded investment is?
Explanation:
'A' [Philips' 12th ed 222]

• One of the best pickling solutions for gypsum-bonded investments is a 50% hydrochloric acid (HCl) solution.
• The HCl aids in the removal of any residual investment, as well as of the oxide coating.
• The disadvantage of HCl is that the fumes from the acid are likely to corrode laboratory metal furnishings.
• In addition, these fumes are a health hazard and should be vented via a fume hood.

Explanation:

Wear is usually undesirable, but under controlled conditions during finishing and polishing procedures, wear is highly beneficial.

Wear is a loss of material resulting from removal and relocation of materials through the contact of two or more materials. When two solid materials are in contact, they touch only at the tips of their highest asperities.

The maximum penetration depth of the laser welding units is 2.5 mm. Since only a small amount of heat is generated, the parts can be handheld during the welding procedure, and welding can be performed close to ceramic or polymeric veneers without causing damage to these materials.

Question: Best way to join cast titanium components is
Explanation:
'A' [Philips' 12th ed 392]

Laser welding in an argon gas atmosphere is a method of choice for joining titanium components of dental prostheses, because the coherent, high-intensity laser pulse of light can be focused in a small region and melt the substrate without extensive microstructural damage to the surrounding areas.

Explanation:

Elastic modulus describes the relative stiffness or rigidity of a material, which is measured by the slope of the elastic region of the stress-strain graph.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Addition silicone material without palladium (H₂ absorber), air bubble formation occurs in cast, which precaution is not taken
Option D: if poured immediately without waiting for 30 min
Explanation:
'D' [Philips' 12th ed 154]

No reaction by-products are formed as long as the correct proportions of divinyl polysiloxane and polymethyl hydrosiloxane are used and there are no impurities. However, the residual polymethyl hydrosiloxane in the material can lead to a secondary reaction with each other or with moisture, to produce hydrogen gas.

Technically, hydrogen gas is a reaction by-product that does not affect the dimensional stability of the impression. Nonetheless, the hydrogen gas evolved can result in pinpoint voids in the gypsum casts poured soon after removal of the impression from the mouth. Manufacturers may add a noble metal, such as palladium, as a scavenger for the released hydrogen gas. The impression should be left overnight if epoxy will be used for pouring models.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: If gypsum mixing is done with boiling water then what should happen to reaction
Option C: reaction will move in reverse direction
Explanation:
'D' [Philips' 12th ed 186]

Little change in setting time occurs between 0°C and 50°C. If the temperature of the plaster-water mixture exceeds 50°C, a gradual retardation occurs.

As the temperature approaches 100°C (boiling water), no reaction takes place. This is the reason why very hot water (near the boiling temperature) is used to wash impurities like calcium chloride and sodium succinate from improved stone powder.

Question: If denture curing is done at the temperatures above 100° C, then porosity is seen in
Explanation:
'A' [Philips' 12th ed 481]

During the polymerization cycle, acrylic dentures probably would yield porosity in thick portions of the denture, since the temperature of the resin exceeds the boiling point of the monomer (100.8°C).

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Main purpose of liner application under zinc phosphate base in an amalgam restoration is?
Explanation:
'A' [Philips' 12th ed 315]

Zinc phosphate cement is an effective base for thermal insulation, but its low pH (acidity) may require a cavity liner under the cement to protect the pulp.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Essential element for chemical reaction when zinc phosphate powder mixed with its liquid is
Explanation:
'C' [Rama Krishna Alla 1st ed 100]

The aluminum of the liquid is essential for the cement formation. The aluminum complexes with the phosphoric acid to form zinc-aluminophosphate gel. Without aluminum, a non-cohesive crystalline matrix of hopeite [Zn₃(Po₄)₂. 4H₂0] would be formed.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: New monomer that improve clinical properties?
Explanation:
'A' [Craig's Restorative Dental Materials 13th ed 165]

Low-Shrink Silorane Monomer:
Traditional composite resins rely upon radical polymerization of methacrylates. A new monomer system called silorane has been developed to reduce shrinkage and internal stress build-up resulting from polymerization. Silorane restorative uses a new ring opening silorane chemistry. Siloranes are a combination of siloxane (known for their hydrophilicity) and oxiranes (known for their low shrinkage and stability).

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Monomer evaporates due to increase in boiling temperature during curing. What will happen?
Explanation:
'A' [Zarb 13th ed 134]

The polymerization reaction is exothermic in nature and should be carefully controlled to avoid a marked increase in temperature, which may exceed the boiling point of unreacted monomer (100.8° C), leading to denture porosity. Gaseous porosity occurs as a result of rapid heating of the flask, leading to monomer evaporation; this appears as fine uniform subsurface spherical pores, localized more often in the thick portion of the denture.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Surface porosity in a denture is due to:
Option B: When temperature of resin is more than its boiling temperature
Explanation:
'B' [Zarb 13th ed 134]

Surface porosity is due to vaporization of monomer when the temperature of resin increases above its boiling point (100.8°C). Surface porosity can trap food, making denture unhygienic and foul smelling.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Which of the following cannot be the reason for difference in shade matching:
Explanation:
'A' [Phillips 12th ed 38]

• Shade selection should occur prior to placement of a rubber dam, because a desiccated tooth appears whiter than a moist or wet tooth.
• Drying the tooth before shade selection makes the tooth appear whiter.
• The most important factor in shade matching is the light source. Shade selection should be made using colour-corrected lights.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Adding a wax reservoir eliminates which kind of porosity?
Explanation:
'C' [Phillips 11th ed 214]

A reservoir should be added to a sprue network to prevent localized shrinkage porosity. When the molten alloy fills the heated casting ring, the pattern area should solidify first and the reservoir last. Because of its large mass of alloy and position in the heat center of the ring, the reservoir remains molten to furnish liquid alloy into the mold as it solidifies.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: GIC mixing time should not exceed-
Explanation:
'D' [Phillips 11th ed 323]

The powder should be incorporated rapidly into the liquid using a stiff spatula for restorative applications or a flexible metal or plastic spatula for luting applications. Normally half of the powder is mixed into the liquid for 5 to 15 seconds; the rest of the powder is then quickly added and mixed by folding the cement on itself until a uniform, glossy appearance is achieved. The mixing time should not exceed 45 seconds but may be less for certain products.

A glossy appearance indicates the presence of unreacted polyacid, which is critical for bonding to the tooth. A dull appearance indicates that the acid has reacted too much with the glass particles for good bonding.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: True about glass transition temperature is -
Option A: Decrease in coefficient of thermal expansion
Option B: Abrupt increase in coefficient of thermal expansion
Option D: Involves long range order arrangement of atoms
Explanation:
'B' [Phillips 11th ed 198]

Glass transition temperature: Temperature above which a sharp increase in the thermal expansion coefficient occurs, indicating increased molecular mobility.

For waxes:
The thermal dimensional change may be affected by the previous treatment of the wax. Thermal expansion of inlay wax increase as a function of temperature. The expansion rate increases abruptly above approximately 35 °C. The temperature at which a change in rate occurs is known as the glass transition temperature. Some constituents of the wax probably change in their crystalline form at this temperature, and the wax is more plastic at higher temperatures.

For acrylic:
The glass transition temperature is a thermal range in which the polymerized resin passes from a soft, rubbery state to a rigid, glassy state. Cooling the denture base resin beyond the glass transition temperature yields a rigid mass.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: In Vita 3D master shade guide, what is the correct sequence of shade selection?
Explanation:
'B' [J Conserv Dent. 2010 Oct-Dec; 13(4): 249–255]

• The Vita 3D-Master shade guide features a systematic colorimetric distribution of 26 shade tabs within the tooth color space.
• The manufacturer purports that this shade guide demonstrates an equidistant distribution in the color space.
• The shade guide is organized into five primary value levels, with a secondary distribution based on chroma and hue.
• These value groups are arranged from the lightest (value level 1) to the darkest (value level 5), left to right. Intermediate shades can be achieved based on mixing formulas.
• The manufacturer advocates a three-step process: value is determined first in making a shade determination and then the chroma and hue are determined.
• The sequence of shade selection is value, then chroma, followed by hue.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Difference in coefficient of thermal expansion between teeth & restoration affects
Explanation:
'A' [Phillip's 11th ed 55]

Coefficient of thermal expansion is defined as the change in length per unit of the original length of the material when its temperature is raised 1°K. A tooth restoration may expand or contract more than the tooth during a change in temperature; thus, there may be marginal leakage adjacent to the restoration or the restoration may debond from the tooth. Restorative materials may change in dimension upto 4.4 times more than the tooth enamel for every degree of temperature change.
